notes.title: The next inflation print, Sep 2026
notes.text: +0.48% on the month, 3.54% year over year (up from 3.35%). Gasoline adds +0.30 points (pump prices are -0.0% this month so far), rents +0.08, everything else +0.10.

notes.title: The inflation path
notes.text: Inflation tops out at 3.74% in Nov 2026 and falls to 2.07% by May 2027. Much of the fall is arithmetic rather than forecast: the largest monthly price rises of the past year drop out of the twelve-month comparison one by one, and those months carry the strongest calls.

notes.title: Oil and the pump
notes.text: Oil is $98 a barrel against $84 in Aug 2026, and the pump price is $4.35 a gallon. In the data since 2000, $1 on a barrel of oil has been worth about 0.03 points on inflation, and pump prices follow oil by a few weeks.

notes.title: Rents and wages
notes.text: Rents in the index follow new-lease rents with about a year's lag; those are up 2.5%, so rents add a steady 0.08 points a month. Wages are up 3.0%, which feeds services prices slowly.

notes.title: Growth this quarter, Q3 2026
notes.text: About +2.9% annualized, estimated from jobs, industrial production, retail sales and jobless claims with 2 of 3 months in. That falls short of the +3.9% pace of the same quarter last year, so year-over-year growth slips to 2.0%.

notes.title: After this quarter
notes.text: The model does not forecast GDP two to four quarters out; every method tried did worse than a constant. It assumes the economy's normal pace, 2.0% a year, adjusted for interest rates. Up or down is then decided by the bar to beat: year-over-year growth rises only in a quarter that grows faster than the same quarter a year earlier, and those bars are already published.

notes.title: Interest rates
notes.text: The Fed funds rate was 3.88% through October 2026, and the market path reaches 4.63% by July 2027. Rate changes reach growth with a lag: about 0.4 points of annual growth per 1 point of change, two to six quarters later. The Fed cut 0.8 points over the last two years, so the cuts still help growth for now; the new hikes start to bite in Q3 2027.

notes.title: The consumer
notes.text: Consumer spending is about two thirds of GDP. Right now consumer spending is +2.6% on a year ago (normal against the last ten years); consumer confidence is 52 (very low against the last ten years); household wealth is +11.8% on a year ago (high against the last ten years); income after inflation is +1.3% (normal against the last ten years); the saving rate is 4.1% of income (low against the last ten years); the 30-year mortgage rate is 7.34%.

drivers.label: Oil (WTI)
drivers.note: Each $1 on a barrel has been worth about 0.03 points on inflation since 2000.

drivers.label: Pump price
drivers.note: Adds +0.30 points to Sep 2026 inflation; pump prices follow oil by a few weeks.

drivers.label: Market rents, new leases
drivers.note: Rents in the index follow with about a year's lag, about 0.08 points a month.

drivers.label: Wages, same people year on year
drivers.note: Median raise for people employed in both periods, so layoffs cannot flatter it. Feeds services prices slowly.

drivers.label: Growth pace, Q3 2026
drivers.note: 2 of 3 months in; year-over-year growth slips to 2.0%.

drivers.label: Pace assumed after this quarter
drivers.note: A normal pace, adjusted for interest rates; the model does not forecast GDP further out.

drivers.label: Fed funds rate
drivers.level: normal against the last ten years
drivers.note: Market path to 4.63% by July 2027; hikes reach growth two to six quarters later, biting from Q3 2027.

drivers.label: Consumer spending
drivers.level: normal against the last ten years
drivers.note: About two thirds of GDP. Very hot spending has been followed by slower growth about 7 times in 10.

drivers.label: Consumer confidence
drivers.level: very low against the last ten years
drivers.note: Very low confidence has not meant weaker growth: the next quarter was higher 63% of the time.

drivers.label: Household wealth
drivers.level: high against the last ten years
drivers.note: Fast wealth gains have meant slowing growth three to four quarters later 61% to 68% of the time.

drivers.label: Income after inflation
drivers.level: normal against the last ten years
drivers.note: Weak real income is the soft spot: spending carried by a low saving rate, not by pay.

drivers.label: Saving rate
drivers.level: low against the last ten years
drivers.note: Extremes carry no measured signal for next quarter, but it is the cushion that is gone when very low.

drivers.label: 30-year mortgage rate
drivers.level: high against the last ten years
drivers.note: Falling mortgage rates have been a strong lead on faster growth (75% to 79%); rising ones a weak lead on slower growth.
